text: Streptococcosis in Nile tilapia (Streptococcus iniae or S. agalactiae) commonly presents with unilateral or bilateral exophthalmia (pop-eye), corneal opacity, abdominal distension, and hemorrhages on the body surface and fin bases. Affected fish often swim erratically in a spiral or corkscrew pattern and become lethargic.
source_title: FAO Cultured Aquatic Species Information Programme - Oreochromis niloticus

text: Behavioral signs of streptococcosis include erratic spiral swimming, loss of equilibrium, gathering near the water outlet, and reduced feed intake. Neurological signs reflect meningoencephalitis caused by the bacterium.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: High water temperature above 26-30 degrees C, high stocking density, and stress from transport or grading strongly predispose tilapia to streptococcosis. Outbreaks peak in warm seasons.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Elevated water temperature above 28 degrees C is a key trigger for streptococcosis; low dissolved oxygen and high ammonia add stress and increase susceptibility.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Neurological signs such as spiral swimming are also seen in Tilapia Lake Virus infection and severe hypoxia, so streptococcosis must be distinguished from these using laboratory confirmation rather than appearance alone.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Confirmation of streptococcosis requires bacterial isolation and culture from brain or kidney on blood agar or TSA, identification of Gram-positive cocci, and PCR for S. iniae or S. agalactiae.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Exophthalmia and body hemorrhages are not specific to streptococcosis; they are also common in Tilapia Lake Virus infection, so visual signs alone cannot reliably separate these two conditions.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Motile Aeromonas septicemia (Aeromonas hydrophila) presents with flank ulcers, scale loss, hemorrhagic and frayed fins, abdominal distension with ascites, and sometimes exophthalmia in Nile tilapia.
source_title: FAO Regional health management guidelines for tilapia

text: Aeromonas septicemia is often a secondary infection following skin damage, poor water quality, high organic load, or stress. Physical injury and high bacterial load in water increase the risk.
source_title: FAO Regional health management guidelines for tilapia

text: High ammonia, low dissolved oxygen, and high organic matter predispose fish to Aeromonas infection; insufficient water exchange markedly raises the risk.
source_title: FAO Regional health management guidelines for tilapia

text: Confirmation of Aeromonas septicemia requires bacterial culture from lesions or kidney on TSA at about 27 degrees C and identification of oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: The hemorrhagic ulcers of Aeromonas septicemia differ from the grey-white necrotic patches of columnaris; the two are distinguished by lesion appearance and laboratory culture.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Immediate safe actions for suspected Aeromonas septicemia include improving water quality (aeration, water exchange, reduced feeding), isolating affected fish, and submitting samples for laboratory confirmation.
source_title: FAO Regional health management guidelines for tilapia

text: Columnaris (Flavobacterium columnare) presents as grey-white necrotic patches on fins, back, or gills, often described as a saddleback lesion, with gill necrosis, whitened mouth, and increased skin mucus.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Columnaris is favored by water temperature above 20 degrees C, high stocking density, mechanical damage, high organic load, and low dissolved oxygen.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: High temperature combined with low dissolved oxygen and high organic load is strongly associated with columnaris outbreaks; water quality fluctuation is a common trigger.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Confirmation of columnaris is done by microscopic examination of lesion scrapings showing haystack-like columns of bacteria and by culture on selective media.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Grey-white necrotic patches of columnaris differ from the cotton-like white growth of fungal (Saprolegnia) infection and from the hemorrhagic ulcers of Aeromonas septicemia.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Gill lesions can also be caused by parasites (Trichodina, Dactylogyrus) and water quality irritation, so microscopy is needed to differentiate these from columnaris gill necrosis.
source_title: WOAH Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals

text: Tilapia Lake Virus (TiLV) disease presents with exophthalmia, darkening of body color, skin hemorrhages and erosion, abdominal distension, and pale gills from anemia.
source_title: WOAH disease card - Tilapia Lake Virus

text: Behavioral signs of TiLV include lethargy, isolation from the school, slow swimming, reduced appetite, and gathering near pond edges.
source_title: WOAH disease card - Tilapia Lake Virus

text: TiLV is favored by water temperature above 25 degrees C, recent introduction of fingerlings or broodstock, high stocking density, and transport stress.
source_title: WOAH disease card - Tilapia Lake Virus

text: TiLV can cause mortality of 20 to 90 percent, especially in juveniles; suspected outbreaks should be reported and the affected stock isolated immediately.
source_title: WOAH disease card - Tilapia Lake Virus

text: Confirmation of TiLV requires RT-PCR on brain, liver, or spleen tissue, virus isolation, or histopathology showing syncytial giant cells.
source_title: WOAH disease card - Tilapia Lake Virus

text: Exophthalmia and hemorrhages in TiLV overlap strongly with streptococcosis; PCR is required to distinguish them, and appearance alone should never be used for a definitive diagnosis.
source_title: WOAH disease card - Tilapia Lake Virus

text: Early TiLV signs are nonspecific and easily confused with streptococcosis or Aeromonas septicemia, so a diagnosis based only on gross appearance is unreliable.
source_title: WOAH disease card - Tilapia Lake Virus

text: Water-quality stress and hypoxia present with surface gasping, rapid gill cover movement, fish gathering at the water inlet or near aeration, and darkened or brownish gills (nitrite toxicity).
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Behavioral signs of water-quality stress include surfacing, erratic darting, jumping, clustering, and rapid breathing, especially at dawn when dissolved oxygen is lowest.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Critical water quality thresholds include dissolved oxygen below 3-4 mg/L, un-ionized ammonia above 0.05 mg/L (acute toxicity), and nitrite above 0.5 mg/L.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Risk factors for hypoxia and ammonia or nitrite stress include high temperature (which lowers dissolved oxygen), overfeeding, filtration or aeration failure, and algal bloom collapse.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Respiratory signs such as gasping and rapid breathing also occur with gill infections (columnaris or parasites), so water quality should be tested first before assuming an infectious cause.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Confirmation of water-quality stress requires on-site testing of dissolved oxygen, ammonia, nitrite, pH, and temperature, and optionally gill tissue examination if an infectious cause is suspected.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia

text: Immediate safe actions for water-quality stress include increasing aeration, partial water exchange, stopping feeding, and reducing stocking density; treat with medication only after testing confirms the cause.
source_title: FAO Health management of Nile tilapia
